structure:
repos/trade-imports-ins-tests on main, the Playwright end-to-end, accessibility, visual and security suite for every trade imports service. One directory per domain under tests/: animals, ins, plants and animals-admin. The scope takes in tests/animals and tests/ins only; tests/plants and tests/animals-admin are left out, as are the plants and animals-admin page objects, flows and domain folders that only they use.

In scope by the numbers: tests/animals holds 127 spec files and 5 READMEs, about 10,600 lines of TypeScript, with 497 literal test() declarations (more at run time, because several specs generate tests in a loop over a table). It is laid out as e2e/pages (21 specs, 2,663 lines: one spec per live-animals journey page), e2e/features (45 specs flat, 3,236 lines, plus features/address-book with 9 specs and 1,732 lines and features/reference-lists with 5 specs and 230 lines), e2e/journeys (7 flat specs and 509 lines, journeys/dynamics with 3 specs and 390 lines, journeys/persistence with 4 specs and 380 lines), e2e/visual (12 specs, 343 lines, with 46 committed PNG baselines beside them in *-snapshots folders), a11y (12 specs, 1,003 lines), security (9 specs, 246 lines, 8 frontend and 1 backend) and cross-browser (a README only, no specs). tests/ins holds 41 spec files, 6 helper modules and 2 READMEs, 3,680 lines, with 173 test() declarations: e2e/features/address-book (19 specs and 6 helpers, 2,257 lines, the largest single area), e2e/features/transporters (4 specs and a runner, 381 lines), e2e/features/notification-type (1 spec, 288 lines), 5 flat e2e/features specs (301 lines: the INS dashboard, page titles, cross-service sessions, organisation scoping and the aggregated notification), a11y (9 specs, 343 lines) and security/address-book (2 specs, 65 lines). tests/ins/cross-browser is a README only.

The suite keeps its support code outside tests/: page-objects/{animals,ins,ins/address-book,shared,shared/auth} (about 2,700 in-scope lines), flows/{animals,ins,shared} (about 1,960 in-scope lines, of which flows/animals/journey.ts is 1,095 and drives most journeys), domain/{animals,ins,shared} (about 1,750 in-scope lines of constants, expected copy, option lists and DB/API/Dynamics models), fixtures/ (7 files, 619 lines: the ui, auth-state, a11y, visual, security and seed-context fixtures), utils/ (16 helpers, 690 lines) and config/ (9 files, 215 lines: base URLs, timeouts, users, service tags, ZAP). Repo-level configuration and documentation sit at the root: playwright.config.ts (CDP target) and playwright.docker-compose.config.ts (local stack target), both with a single chromium project; package.json's 24 test scripts, which are how a domain and test type are selected; README.md (666 lines, with the per-domain and per-environment script and PROFILE tables); AGENTS.md; docs/{animals-journey,a11y,security,cross-browser}.md; .github/workflows; bin/ seeding and probe scripts; zap/ automation files. There is no rulings or decisions ledger in the repo: no spec/decisions.json, no decisions file anywhere outside node_modules, so the only rulings this source carries are the ones its docs and READMEs state in prose.

The committed PNG visual baselines are binary and are not read as text; the visual specs name them, and the part that owns those specs claims what each baseline is taken of and under what viewport and state, not the pixels.

Cut into 16 parts: 11 over tests/animals (3 by journey page group, 3 by feature group, 1 for the animals-side address book, 1 for end-to-end journeys and reference lists, 1 for persistence and Dynamics, 1 for accessibility, 1 for visual and security), 4 over tests/ins (2 for the address book, 1 for the dashboard and notification type, 1 for transporters with INS accessibility and security) and 1 for the suite's own configuration, scripts and documentation. Page objects, flows, domain constants, fixtures and utils are read as full context by whichever parts' specs use them, and several parts therefore name the same support file; a claim comes from a test, so a support file read by two parts yields no duplicate claim.

A newly created notification is DRAFT, and reading its fulfilments back reports the same reference number, the DRAFT status and an empty fulfilments list when it was created without one.
claims.note: A notification submitted without an ITAHC is allowed: the test's title names that case and no refusal follows.

claims.statement: Submitting a draft moves it to SUBMITTED, and its fulfilments read back reports SUBMITTED too.
claims.note: Submitting takes the notification's concurrency token, so a stale copy cannot submit it.

claims.statement: Amending a submitted notification moves it to AMEND, and its fulfilments read back reports AMEND.
Cancelling an amendment returns the notification to SUBMITTED.
claims.quote:
const cancelled = await notificationApi.cancelAmendNotification(id);
    expect(cancelled.status).toBe(notificationStatuses.submitted);

claims.statement: Copying a submitted notification twice produces two new notifications, each with its own reference number different from the original's and from each other's, and each starting as DRAFT.
claims.note: Both copies are taken with the same concurrency token, so copying does not consume it.

claims.statement: Deleting a notification moves it to DELETED, and deleting it again leaves it DELETED rather than failing.
A submitted notification's view is read-only: its heading is the notification reference, its status tag reads "Submitted", and the page offers no "Change" link.
A notification reference takes the form GBN-<letters>-<two digits>-<six letters or digits>, and it is the view's level-1 heading.
Amending a submitted notification from the dashboard opens a page headed "Review your notification" whose status tag reads "Amend".
Amend is reached from the notification list: the trader opens the dashboard, searches for the reference and follows the Amend action on that notification.
"Back" on a submitted notification's view, opened from the notification list, returns to the notification list.
"Back" on an amendment review opened by the Amend action returns to the dashboard.
The back link on a notification view is a link named exactly "Back", not a button.

claims.statement: A submission event is published under the event type NotificationSubmitted, with a schema version and a schema URL under schemas.defra.gov.uk naming the event and its version.

An outbox event can carry the actor who caused it — an id, a source, a user type, a display name, an organisation id and an organisation acted on behalf of — and a list of status changes, each a status, the date it changed and the actor who changed it.
The notification published to other services is a GBN-AG document with two halves: an exchanged document and a specified consignment.

The published exchanged document carries the notification's identifier, the trader's own assigned id, a notification status code, a version id, an issue date and time, the issuer, a list of signed clauses, and a list of referenced documents.

The published specified consignment carries the consignor, consignee, despatch, delivery, importer and carrier parties, the origin country, the unloading base port, the final destination, the main carriage transport movements, the transit countries, whether the consignment holds unweaned animals, and the consignment items.

A published trade line item carries a description, the scientific and common species names, a product unit quantity per delivery, an item quantity per package, and the individual animals, each with a name and a list of identifiers.
Each animal identifier is published as a type code and a content value, so the kind of identifier (ear tag, passport and so on) travels as a code beside the number.
claims.note: notification-data-gaps.spec.ts:86 and :120 name EAR_TAG and PASSPORT as two of those type codes.

claims.statement: A published party carries an identifier, a URL id, a name, a party role code and a list of party type codes, each coded value being a value with an optional URL id and name.

A published country carries a code, its subordinate country sub-divisions and a region of origin code; a published location carries an identifier, a URL id, a name and a type code; and a published transport movement carries a numeric mode code and the transport contract documents.

The canned submission event the suite keeps carries a flat summary of the notification — reference number, status, point of entry and a commodities list of species name and number of animals — not the GBN-AG document the outbox event model describes.
claims.note: An ambiguity recorded, not settled: outbox-event-document.ts:9 types `data` as GbnAgEventData, and the canned file also carries an eventId and a publishedAt that the model does not. The reconciler should decide which shape is current.

claims.statement: The security scan is dynamic application security testing with OWASP ZAP as a proxy: Playwright drives real signed-in journeys through it instead of letting ZAP crawl, so ZAP attacks what a real session touched.
claims.quote: A DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) scan using [OWASP ZAP](https://www.zaproxy.org/) as a proxy. Playwright drives real authenticated journeys through it rather than letting ZAP crawl, so it observes what a real session touches and then attacks that.

claims.statement: Scan coverage is traffic-driven, so any route no spec drives is invisible to the scan; the attacking corpus is therefore curated by hand rather than generated.
claims.quote: Coverage is therefore **traffic-driven**: a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan. That is why the `@active` corpus is curated by hand rather than generated.
claims.note: Stated in general terms: the weakness is one of coverage, not of any particular route.

claims.statement: There are two security profiles: a passive one that runs the end-to-end suite without the attacking specs and does not attack, and an attacking one that runs only the attacking specs and is deliberate and docker-compose only.
claims.quote:
| `security`        | The e2e suite, excluding `@active` | No — passive only | Cheap, run broadly              |
| `security:active` | The `@active` suite only           | Yes               | Deliberate; docker-compose only |

claims.statement: The attacking specs are kept out of the passive profile because they walk the same journeys a second time and include destructive steps.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, note under the Profiles table
claims.quote: `@active` is excluded from the passive profile because it walks the same journeys a second time and includes destructive steps.

claims.statement: The attacking profile is refused on the CDP platform: the attacking specs delete notifications, documents and dead-letter messages and the scan refires each with fuzzed payloads, which is acceptable against a throwaway stack and destructive against a shared one, so the entrypoint fails the run instead.
claims.quote: The `@active` suite deletes notifications, documents and DLQ messages, and the active scan re-fires each with fuzzed payloads — fine against a disposable stack, destructive against a shared one. `entrypoint.sh` writes to `FAILED` rather than running it.

claims.statement: Guarding only the production environment is not enough to keep the attacking profile off shared environments, because such a guard would still have let dev, test and perf-test run it.
claims.quote: The `throwIfProdEnvironment` guard is no help here: it stops `prod` alone, so `dev`, `test` and `perf-test` would all have run.

claims.statement: The scan runs in three lanes that do not share a configuration or a target: locally against the localhost stack in either profile, from a GitHub Action against a stack on the runner in the attacking profile, and on the CDP portal against a deployed environment in the passive profile only.
claims.quote: | **CDP portal**    | `PROFILE` env var → `entrypoint.sh`                                                                         | `playwright.config.ts`                | deployed `${ENVIRONMENT}` | `security` or `<domain>:security` only  |

claims.statement: The GitHub Action that runs the attacking scan is manual dispatch only and its nightly schedule stays switched off until an end-to-end run has been verified.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, paragraph after the lanes table
claims.quote: The GitHub Action is manual dispatch only; the nightly schedule stays disabled pending a verified end-to-end run.

claims.statement: The attacking scan's report is published to a public GitHub Pages site under a dated path and is password-protected for that reason, and reports older than seven days are deleted.
claims.quote: Its report publishes to GitHub Pages under `security-active/<date>/`, password-protected via the `ZAP_REPORT_PASSWORD` secret because that Pages site is otherwise public. Reports older than 7 days are pruned.
claims.note: The password itself is a repository secret and is not in the source; nothing here names a value.

claims.statement: Six services are in the scan, each as its own named ZAP context: the animals frontend, the animals admin, the INS frontend, the animals backend, the plants backend and the address book.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'What gets scanned' table, and zap/automation-context.yaml env.contexts
claims.quote:
| `trade-imports-animals-frontend` | 3000       | `frontend`        |
| `trade-imports-animals-admin`    | 3001       | `admin`           |
| `trade-imports-ins-frontend`     | 3002       | `ins`             |
| `trade-imports-animals-backend`  | 8085       | `animals-backend` |
| `trade-imports-plants-backend`   | 8091       | `plants-backend`  |
| `trade-imports-address-book`     | 8089       | `address-book`    |

claims.statement: Each context's address is supplied by its own environment variable rather than hard-coded, so the same plans point at the compose stack's ports locally and at a per-service subdomain on CDP.
claims.ref: zap/automation-context.yaml env.contexts urls; docs/security.md, 'Ports are the compose stack's'
claims.quote: Ports are the compose stack's; on CDP each service is a per-service subdomain.

claims.statement: Diagnostic endpoints are left out of every context rather than scanned: health and static assets on the three Node apps, and health, info, metrics, cache and env on the three Java services.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'Diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned'; zap/automation-context.yaml excludePaths for every context
claims.quote: Diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned: `/health` and static assets on the Node contexts, and the full actuator set (`/health`, `/info`, `/metrics`, `/cache`, `/env`) on the three Java services.
claims.note: The Java services' diagnostic endpoints sit on the API's own root namespace, not under a prefix, because the actuator base path is "/" in each service's own configuration.

claims.statement: The identifiers in a page or API address are declared to ZAP as data rather than structure, so each run's notification does not appear as a brand-new branch of the site tree and the identifier itself becomes something the scan can attack: the notification id and upload id on the animals frontend, the address id on the INS frontend, the reference number and upload id on the animals backend, the reference number on the plants backend, and the organisation id and address id on the address book.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml env.contexts structure.dataDrivenNodes (every context), with the frontend comment at lines 15-21
claims.quote:
dataDrivenNodes tells ZAP the segment
    # is data, not structure: one folded node, and the id becomes an
    # injection point (IDOR-style access-by-id checks included).
claims.note: This is how the suite tests for access to another organisation's record by guessing its identifier.

claims.statement: Those structure rules only apply to parts of the site tree as they are first seen, so the contexts are registered on ZAP by a plan of their own before any journey runs; registering them with the scanning plan afterwards would be too late for the identifiers to be recognised as data.
claims.quote:
Structural Modifiers (dataDrivenNodes) and excludePaths only apply to
# site-tree nodes as they're *added* — they don't retroactively reshape
# nodes that already exist.

claims.statement: The context-registration plan declares one do-nothing job only because a plan must have at least one, there being no traffic yet to wait for.
claims.quote:
# No traffic exists yet at this point in the run, so there's nothing to
  # wait for — this job only exists because a plan needs at least one job.

claims.statement: All three ZAP plans must declare exactly the same contexts, and a run stops with an explanatory error before registering anything if they have drifted apart, because ZAP offers no way to share that block between plans.
claims.quote: `env.contexts in ${mismatches.join(', ')} doesn't match ${BASELINE_FILE} — ZAP has no way to share this block across plans, so all three must be kept identical.`

claims.statement: The attacking plan runs one attack job per context, six in all, each capped at 60 minutes.
claims.quote:
- type: activeScan
    parameters:
      context: frontend
      ... 
      maxScanDurationInMins: 60
claims.note: Quote abbreviated across the job's comment block; the same two parameters appear on each of the six jobs.

claims.statement: The 60-minute cap is a runaway guard rather than a budget, set at about four and a half times the slowest context measured: the animals frontend took 13 minutes 27 seconds, the admin 4 minutes 39, the INS frontend 1 minute 25, the backend 1 minute 17 and the address book 21 seconds, 21 minutes in all.
claims.quote:
A runaway guard, not a budget. Measured: frontend 13m27s, admin 4m39s,
      # ins 1m25s, backend 1m17s, address-book 21s — 21m total, frontend 64% of
      # it. 60 is ~4.5x the slowest, leaving room for CI (2 vCPU, ~2-3x local)
      # and for the corpus to roughly double.

claims.statement: The cap in the plan and the figure the gate checks against must be changed together and must match exactly, or a cut-short scan would pass unnoticed.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml, frontend activeScan comment; utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts, ACTIVE_SCAN_CAP_MINS
claims.quote:
Change this, the six below, and ACTIVE_SCAN_CAP_MINS in
      # utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts together — they must match exactly.

claims.statement: A run fails when an attack job finished at or within half a minute of its cap, because a scan cut off part-way reporting no findings is a false clean; the fix is to raise the cap, not to overlook it.
A run fails when a declared context recorded no traffic at all, the one failure that looks like success, since nothing reached means no site-tree entry, no alerts and a clean-looking report section.
claims.quote:
Fails the run when a declared context recorded no traffic — the one failure
 * mode that looks like success, since no requests means no site-tree node, no
 * alerts, and a clean-looking report section.
claims.note: The check reads the plan rather than the report, because a context with no traffic is missing from the report entirely. It catches a context nothing drives, a spec dropped from the corpus, and the case where the API clients stop sending through the proxy.

claims.statement: The no-traffic check only runs in the attacking profile.
claims.quote: const contextsWithNoTraffic = zapProfile === 'active' ? await findContextsWithNoTraffic(client, scope?.contexts) : [];

claims.statement: An attacking run can be narrowed to one domain, and then only that domain's contexts are checked for traffic and the report is marked as a scoped run so a green scoped report is never mistaken for a full one: animals covers the animals frontend and backend, animals-admin the admin, ins the INS frontend and address book, and plants the plants backend.
claims.ref: config/zap.ts, ZAP_SCOPE_CONTEXTS and resolveZapScope; utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts, scopedSection

claims.statement: An unknown domain name for a scoped run is refused with a message listing the domains that exist, rather than silently scanning everything.
claims.quote: throw new Error(`Unknown ZAP_SCOPE '${domain}'. Expected one of: ${Object.keys(ZAP_SCOPE_CONTEXTS).join(', ')}`);

claims.statement: Anything other than the exact attacking profile name is treated as passive, so a mistyped profile cannot start an attack.
Each ZAP alert type is rated from a rules file that maps ZAP's plugin ids to ignore, warn or fail, and an unlisted alert fails the build if it is high risk and only warns otherwise.
claims.quote:
Unlisted rules default to: FAIL if High risk, WARN otherwise — see
# run-and-gate.ts.
claims.note: High is chosen as the bar because it is the least noisy risk tier and so the safest starting point for a new gate; individual medium findings are to be escalated in the rules file as they are triaged.

claims.statement: An ignored alert stays visible in the report exactly as a warned one does and the difference is documentation only: it records that someone has already looked at it and judged it a known false positive.
claims.quote:
IGNORE: triaged as a known false positive — stays visible in the report
#   (same as WARN) and does not fail the build; the difference from WARN is
#   documentation only, marking that someone has already looked at it

claims.statement: No alert is suppressed or ignored today: the rules file holds its format, its defaults and two commented-out examples, and not one live rule line.
claims.ref: zap/rules.tsv, whole file (every line begins with #)
claims.quote:
# Examples:
# 10015	WARN	(Incomplete or No Cache-control and Pragma HTTP Header Set — flagged 2026-08-19, not yet triaged)
# 10096	IGNORE	(Timestamp Disclosure - Unix — triaged 2026-08-19, false positive: matches the numeric suffix of a notification reference number, not an actual timestamp)
claims.note: The two examples name findings previously seen on this suite, but as examples only: with no live line, every alert today is rated by the default rule.

claims.statement: The gate counts a failing finding once per alert type rather than once per occurrence, so a finding seen on eighty-one pages is one thing to fix.
claims.quote:
Gated per alert type, not per instance — an 81-instance finding that
    // fails the gate is one thing to fix, not 81.

claims.statement: A finding recorded twice because ZAP split one host into two entries of its site tree is counted once, while the same finding on two genuinely different hosts still counts twice.
claims.note: mechanism: groups the report's site entries by name and keeps one alert per plugin id in each group.

claims.statement: Alongside its alerts each site in the report shows how many requests reached it, as reassurance that a site with few or no findings was really reached through the proxy rather than quietly skipped.
claims.ref: utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts, getMessageCount comment and the index page's Sites table

claims.statement: Each run writes a landing page with a row per site showing pass or fail, requests seen and the count of high, medium, low and informational alerts, plus a totals row, and links to the full human-readable report, the machine-readable one, the Playwright run's own report and ZAP's log.
claims.quote: Sites
claims.note: mechanism: builds the HTML landing page the CDP report viewer links to, from the report JSON and live request counts.

claims.statement: The landing page is written before the run is failed, so the report exists on disk exactly when someone needs it most.
claims.quote:
Written before the throw below, not after — a failing run is exactly

claims.statement: The landing page carries a prominent notice in three cases: a scan that hit its cap, a run whose traffic-generating specs did not all pass, and a run narrowed to one domain, the first two as failures and the third as a warning.
claims.quote: The traffic-generation specs did not all succeed (outcome: ${specsOutcome}) — the findings below reflect whatever traffic ran before that, not full corpus coverage.

claims.statement: ZAP's own log and its machine-readable report are republished as plain HTML pages, because the CDP report viewer refuses anything that is not HTML and the GitHub Action's password gate only wraps HTML files.
claims.ref: utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts, ZAP_LOG_ARTEFACT and JSON_REPORT_ARTEFACT comment with wrapAsHtml

claims.statement: Both scanning plans produce one combined report, machine-readable and human-readable, covering every site ZAP touched in the session, with no filter by site.
claims.ref: zap/automation-passive.yaml and zap/automation-active.yaml, the two report jobs
claims.quote: # No sites: filter — covers every site ZAP touched this session.
claims.note: Both plans title the report 'trade-imports-animals — security scan' even though it covers six services.

claims.statement: The plans wait for passive scanning and then pause five seconds before attacking or reporting, because ZAP registers the last site a moment after the last journey finishes navigating and would otherwise reject it as an invalid site.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml and zap/automation-passive.yaml, passiveScan-wait and delay jobs
claims.quote:
ZAP's site-tree bookkeeping lags slightly behind the last spec to finish
  # navigating — without this, the activeScan jobs below can start before

claims.statement: The DOM-based cross-site-scripting rule is switched off on every attack job, because it needs a real browser the plain ZAP image does not ship, is far slower than the other rules, and is a poor fit for server-rendered GOV.UK Design System pages that keep client-side DOM handling to a minimum; the reflected and stored cross-site-scripting rules still run.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml, the policyDefinition on each of the six activeScan jobs
claims.quote:
Reflected/
    # stored XSS rules are unaffected and still run. Also a poor fit for
    # this app regardless: GOV.UK Design System + Nunjucks server-rendered
    # pages, GDS progressive enhancement keeps client-side DOM handling to a
    # minimum, so DOM-based XSS is a small slice of the real risk surface.

claims.statement: The passive plan carries no attack job at all and is safe to run against a real deployed environment on demand.
claims.quote:
ZAP Automation Framework plan — passive scan only, no activeScan jobs.
# Safe to run against a real deployed environment on demand, no destructive
# risk.

claims.statement: Deciding pass or fail is deliberately kept out of the ZAP plans and done afterwards by the suite's own gate, so the plans only scan and report.
claims.quote:
Gating is deliberately not done here; see
# run-and-gate.ts and rules.tsv.

claims.statement: The scan is run against the already-running ZAP rather than a fresh one, so it sees what passive scanning captured while the journeys ran.

A plan that reports an error of its own fails the run, and a plan that has not finished within five hours is abandoned with an error, that ceiling being a safety net over the worst case rather than a coverage limit.
claims.quote: throw new Error(`ZAP automation plan finished with errors: ${progress.error.join('; ')}`);

claims.statement: The suite talks to ZAP on a loopback address through a connection that ignores any proxy settings in the environment, so the platform's own outbound proxy cannot redirect those control calls.
claims.quote:
Dedicated agent with no proxyEnv so CDP's HTTP_PROXY / --use-env-proxy
// cannot redirect these loopback API calls.

claims.statement: ZAP listens on a port kept deliberately outside the workspace's two growing port ranges, because the next free slot after either range is eventually taken by the next new service.
The suite's ZAP credential and port both fall back to built-in local development values when nothing is set, so no one has to configure them day to day.
claims.quote: export const zapApiKey = process.env.ZAP_API_KEY || '[REDACTED]';
claims.note: The default value is redacted here on principle; it is a local development placeholder, not a real credential. Stated in general terms: a built-in default exists, and the environment variable overrides it.

claims.statement: The three APIs are scanned without any attacking spec of their own because every API client in the suite is built from Playwright's own request fixture, which inherits the run's proxy, so the specs' seeding and assertion calls reach ZAP as real traffic.
claims.quote: The three APIs are scanned all the same: every API client here is built from Playwright's own `request` fixture, which inherits the project's proxy, so the specs' seeding and assertion calls reach ZAP as real traffic.

claims.statement: A security spec that needs to call the notification API through the proxy explicitly gets a client pointed at ZAP, rather than relying on inheritance.
claims.quote:
const context = await request.newContext({ proxy: { server: `http://localhost:${zapPort}` } });
    await use(new NotificationApiClient(context));

claims.statement: The sign-in stub is deliberately observed but never attacked, because it is a temporary service the team does not own, while the service's own sign-in and sign-in-callback handlers are in scope since the callback and its redirect parameter outlive the stub.

claims.quote: A temporary sign-in stub we do not own. Observed passively, never attacked. Our own `/auth/sign-in` and `/auth/sign-in-oidc` handlers **are** in scope — the OIDC callback and its `redirect` parameter outlive the stub.

claims.statement: The platform's file uploader is out of scope because the browser posts uploads to the frontend, which forwards them from the server, so the uploader never enters ZAP's site tree.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'What is not, and why' table
claims.quote: A platform component. The browser posts uploads to the frontend, which forwards them server-side, so the uploader never enters the site tree.

claims.statement: The INS backend is out of scope because it is a queue consumer with no HTTP controllers: its risk boundary is the queue, which this kind of scan cannot reach, and the API that produces its events is scanned instead.

claims.quote: An SQS consumer with no HTTP controllers. Its risk boundary is the queue, which DAST cannot reach; the API that produces those events is scanned.

claims.statement: From a workspace clone the docker-compose run stops before the first test unless that clone owns the stack, naming the owning clone and offering GitHub Actions instead; ALLOW_FOREIGN_STACK=1 runs anyway, and a checkout outside a workspace, such as the tests image, is never stopped.

owns the stack (`tim docker owner` in the workspace prints the owner). From
another clone it stops before the first test with "The stack belongs to
`<clone>`. Run E2E there, or push and let GitHub Actions run it." Set
`ALLOW_FOREIGN_STACK=1` to run anyway. A checkout outside a workspace, such as
the tests image, is never stopped.

claims.statement: The animals journey accessibility scans leave out govuk-frontend's two conditional-reveal radio groups, because govuk-frontend sets aria-expanded on each radio that opens a reveal and axe's aria-allowed-attr rule rejects it — a disagreement between govuk-frontend and axe rather than a service defect.
claims.quote:
The animals journey scans leave out govuk-frontend's conditional-reveal radios
(`govukConditionalRevealRadioOnOrigin` and
`govukConditionalRevealRadiosOnReason` in `fixtures/a11y.ts`). govuk-frontend sets `aria-expanded` on
each radio that opens a conditional reveal (`radios.mjs`), and axe's
`aria-allowed-attr` rule rejects it. That is a disagreement between
govuk-frontend and axe, not a service defect.

claims.statement: A CDP run gives each test 60 seconds and each expectation 15 seconds, while a docker-compose run keeps Playwright's 30-second and 5-second defaults, because each CDP page load is a real network hop.
claims.quote:
The CDP config sets a 60s test timeout and a 15s expect timeout, against
Playwright's 30s and 5s defaults that the docker-compose config keeps. Each CDP
page load is a real network hop, so CDP needs a longer budget than the local
stack.

claims.statement: A leaked address book on the dev environment, grown to 4,882 records, made every contact-address page load fan out dozens of concurrent reads through the CDP SSL sidecar, which returned 502 and 504 responses for minutes at a time; session reuse, a per-test address-book teardown and a one-off purge removed the leak, and three clean runs then kept every test under three-quarters of its budget, so the CDP test timeout came down from 90 to 60 seconds.
claims.quote:
The suite once also timed out in bursts: a
leaked address book on dev (grown to 4,882 records) made every
`contact-address` page load fan out dozens of concurrent reads through the
CDP SSL sidecar, which returned 502/504s for a few minutes at a time. Session
reuse, a per-test address-book teardown and a one-off purge removed the leak
and the outage; three clean CDP runs then kept every test under
three-quarters of its new budget (45s, or 135s for tests marked
`test.slow()`), so the timeout came down from 90s to 60s.

claims.statement: The fifteen-document limits test sets its own 120-second timeout, because its real uploads and virus scans take 57 to 60 seconds on the local stack and about 67 seconds on CDP.
claims.quote:
`documents-limits`' fifteen-document test sets its own 120s timeout: its real
uploads and virus scans take 57–60s on the local stack and about 67s on CDP,
which left too thin a margin under the 90s a slow test gets on compose.
Re-check it if the base timeouts change.

claims.statement: Each flow step waits up to 30 seconds for its page's heading rather than for the test timeout, so a transient 502 fails the step that hit it and names the page it was waiting for.
claims.quote:
The flow helpers wait for each page's heading with `pageLoadWait`
(`config/timeouts.ts`, 30s) rather than the test timeout, so a transient 502
fails the step that hit it within 30s and names the page it was waiting for.

The `addressBookApi` and `isolatedOrganisationAddressBookApi` fixtures delete
every address and transporter created through them once the test ends, pass or
fail, retries included.

claims.statement: A transporter saved through the user interface is only deleted if the spec tracks it by name, and an address added on the add-address page or through the handshake is not deleted at all.

A record a test saves through the UI is not created
through them: call `addressBookApi.trackTransporterNamed(name)` after saving a
transporter so it is deleted too. A delete that fails is logged with the
record's id and never fails the test. Records saved through the UI in any other
way, such as an address added on the add-address page or through the
handshake, are not deleted.

claims.statement: In CDP dev, test, perf-test and ext-test the address book removes every address about seven days after it was created, which needs both ADDRESS_TTL_DAYS and ADDRESS_TTL_EXPIRY_ENABLED set; the local docker-compose stack sets neither.

address about 7 days after it was created. That needs both `ADDRESS_TTL_DAYS`
and `ADDRESS_TTL_EXPIRY_ENABLED` set; the local docker-compose stack sets

only this run's record.

seeded in `globalSetup` expire too; the next run's `ensureE2eAddressBook`
creates them again. `globalSetup` seeds them through its own client, so no
test's clean-up deletes them.

using one of the shared journey addresses, because every spec running
alongside it reads those.

so that is the one way through the services alone to copy an address the
notification refuses.

claims.statement: CDP blocks direct calls to its back-end services from outside its network, so a laptop run sets CDP_LOCAL=true, which sends those calls through the protected ephemeral gateway and needs a developer API key sent as x-api-key; the run stops at once if the key is missing, and a CDP Portal run needs neither setting.

global set-up cannot reach the backend or the address book without

ephemeral gateway, which needs `DEVELOPER_API_KEY` as `x-api-key`. The run
stops at once if `CDP_LOCAL=true` and the key is missing. The CDP Portal run
sits inside CDP and needs neither.

claims.statement: A service tag is a different kind of tag: it names a service whose pull request should also run the spec, whatever test type or domain the spec sits in.
claims.quote:
A service tag, such as
`@ins-backend`, is a different kind: it names a service whose pull request
should also run the spec, whatever test type or domain the spec is in (see
[GitHub Actions workflow](#github-actions-workflow)).

claims.statement: The suite recognises eight service tags, each belonging to the domains that already run it by path: @address-book, @ins-backend and @ins-frontend to ins; @animals-admin to animals-admin; @animals-backend to animals and animals-admin; @animals-frontend to animals; and @plants-backend and @plants-frontend to plants.
Linting fails a spec whose tags disagree with its test-type directory: a spec under a11y/ must carry @a11y, one under security/ must carry @active, and one under e2e/ must carry neither.
claims.quote:
`npm run lint` runs `lint:suite-tags` to keep the two in step: a test under `a11y/` must carry
`@a11y`, one under `security/` must carry `@active`, and one under `e2e/` neither.

claims.statement: Linting fails a spec that carries the service tag of a service whose pull request already runs the spec's own domain by path.
claims.quote: `npm run lint` fails if a spec carries the tag of a service whose pull request already runs the spec's domain by path, as `config/service-tags.ts` maps it.

claims.statement: The tag check asks Playwright to list the tests so it reads the tags a test really has, title, describe and test tags merged, and needs no stack, sign-in or browser.
claims.quote:
Asks Playwright to list the tests, so it sees the tags a test really has
 * (title, describe and test tags merged). Needs no stack, sign-in or browser.

claims.statement: The tag check names each offending test by file, line and title with what is wrong, exits non-zero when there is any, and otherwise reports how many tests it checked.

The reason the tag rules are enforced is that a spec under security/ without @active would run in every end-to-end and pull-request check, and one under a11y/ without @a11y would run in end-to-end and be missed by the accessibility run.
claims.quote:
Test types are selected by tag, not by directory: `npm test` runs a domain's
 * whole directory minus `@a11y`, `@active`, `@compose` and `@dynamics`. So a
 * spec under security/ without `@active` would run in every e2e and PR check,
 * and one under a11y/ without `@a11y` would run in e2e and be missed by the
 * a11y run.

claims.statement: @duplicated-in-frontend marks an end-to-end spec whose behaviour the frontend's own FIT suite also proves, so a reader knows the check exists in both places.
claims.quote: `@duplicated-in-frontend` marks an end-to-end spec whose behaviour the frontend's own FIT suite also proves, so a reader knows the check exists in both places.

claims.statement: The suite does not wipe the database before it runs and does not need to, because every spec creates the state it asserts on through the back-end API, scoped to that run, so the specs pass against a database holding earlier runs' records.
claims.quote:
The suite does not wipe the database before it runs, and does not need to.
Every spec creates the state it asserts on through the front door (the
backend API), scoped to that run, so the specs pass against a database that
already holds the records of earlier runs.

claims.statement: A spec asserts which journey page is open through the page object's expected URL pattern, which matches the page whichever trail its address carries, and asserts an exact trail through the on-trail pattern or exact URL built from the page objects' own slugs; a spec never types a from query itself.
claims.quote:
- Which page is open: the page object's `expectedUrlPattern(reference)`. It matches the page whichever trail its address carries.
- The exact trail: the page object's `expectedUrlPatternOnTrail(reference, places)` for a `toHaveURL` matcher, or `expectedUrlOnTrail(reference, places)` for an exact `href` value. Pass the page objects' own `slug`s and the `TRAIL_START` places. A spec never types a `?from=` query.

claims.statement: An assertion two specs share lives in a shared checks module, and a flow or page object holds no assertion.
claims.quote: - An assertion two specs share lives in a `*-checks.ts` module under `page-objects/shared/` (`journey-checks.ts`, `type-ahead-checks.ts`). A flow or page object holds no assertion.

claims.statement: Visual regression tests guard rendered composition — layout, spacing, colour and typography as the user sees the page — by comparing screenshots against committed baseline images and failing if any pixels differ outside the masked regions.
claims.quote: Visual regression tests (tagged `@visual`) guard rendered composition — layout, spacing, colour, and typography as the user sees the page. They compare screenshots against committed baseline images and fail if any pixels differ outside the masked regions.

claims.statement: Baselines are committed beside their spec files, and each platform needs its own baseline, both of which are updated when a visual change is intentional.
claims.quote: Baselines are stored alongside their spec files in `*-snapshots/` directories and must be committed. Each platform requires its own baseline — update both when visual changes are intentional.

claims.statement: Visual specs run headless whatever the project setting, because headed mode uses the operating system's font rendering, which produces pixel differences against a headless baseline.
claims.quote: Visual specs run headless whatever the project setting, because headed mode uses OS font rendering, which produces pixel differences against a headless baseline.

claims.statement: On macOS a visual run launches the browser itself with legacy scroll bars, because Chromium sizes a native select's arrow box from the macOS scroll bar style and overlay scroll bars draw every native select four pixels narrower, which failed a baseline made on a trackpad once a mouse was plugged in.
claims.quote: Visual specs import `test` from `@fixtures/visual`. On macOS it launches Playwright's headless shell with legacy scroll bars (`-AppleShowScrollBars Always`) and connects to it over CDP. Chromium sizes a native `<select>` arrow box from the macOS scroll bar style, and with the default "Show scroll bars: Automatically" setting that style follows whether a mouse is connected: overlay scroll bars on a trackpad alone, legacy ones with a mouse. Overlay scroll bars draw every native select 4px narrower, so a `*-darwin.png` baseline made on a laptop's trackpad failed with a mouse plugged in (704 pixels on the no-JavaScript import reason page), and the other way round. Playwright's own launch refuses an argument that does not start with `-`, so the fixture starts the browser itself. On Linux the fixture is the shared one, unchanged.
claims.note: mechanism: the visual fixture's own browser launch, for the macOS baseline. Names the no-JavaScript import reason page as the page whose baseline differed.

claims.statement: The declaration visual specs set the date of declaration to a fixed string before the screenshot rather than masking it, because the server writes today's date into the page text and a mask is as wide as that text; the date's strong emphasis is proved by the declaration end-to-end specs instead.
claims.quote: The declaration specs set the date of declaration to a fixed string before the screenshot instead of masking it, because the server writes today's date into the page text and a mask is as wide as that text, which changes with the day and month. `freezeDatePickersAt` does not reach that text: it stops the browser clock and moves each date picker's served bounds, and changes nothing the server has already written. The date's strong emphasis is proved by the declaration e2e specs.

claims.statement: Only the animals and plants domains have visual specs.
claims.quote: `animals` and `plants` have `@visual` specs.

claims.statement: Baselines are regenerated by two commands, one for the host-rendered darwin image and one for the container-rendered linux image CI uses, each running every visual spec and writing the updated snapshot into the working tree for commit.

Regenerate the E2E baseline against the stack frontend with
`npm run test:visual:update:macos` for the host-rendered `*-darwin.png` image and
`npm run test:visual:update:linux` for the container-rendered `*-linux.png` image
used by CI. Both commands run every `@visual` spec and write the
updated snapshot into the working tree for commit.

claims.statement: The Linux baseline script points the service URLs at host.docker.internal and maps localhost to the host, because inside the container localhost is the container.
claims.quote: The Linux script points the service URLs at `host.docker.internal`, because inside the container `localhost` is the container. It also runs the container with `--add-host=localhost:host-gateway`, which maps `localhost` to the host, so any URL the script does not override and that still names `localhost` reaches the stack too.

Every full-page screenshot of a notification page masks the whole status strip. It renders

whole strip is masked, not the reference alone, so the masked box stays a fixed size. The

claims.statement: A calendar screenshot depends on today's date twice — the browser's today picks the month and highlighted day, and the server's today sets each picker's minimum and maximum date — so the suite stops the browser clock on a fixed day and moves the served bounds by the same number of days.
claims.quote:
A calendar screenshot depends on today's date twice: the browser's today picks the month and
the highlighted day, and the server's today sets each picker's `data-min-date` and
`data-max-date`. `freezeDatePickersAt` (`utils/frozen-date-picker.ts`) stops the browser clock
on a fixed day and moves the served bounds by the same number of days, so the calendar looks
as it would if that day were today.

claims.quote: Coverage is therefore **traffic-driven**: a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan. That is why the `@active` corpus is curated by hand rather than generated.

| `security:active` | The `@active` suite only           | Yes               | Deliberate; docker-compose only |

claims.quote: - `toCommercialTransporter` follows the add route's commercial arm: the list first, then the transporter type question, then the form for a commercial transporter that is not on the list.

claims.statement: Saving a private transporter's add form lands back on the transporter list with the new transporter first and chosen.
claims.quote: - `fillAndSavePrivateTransporterAddForm` fills the open private transporter form with the details given and saves it, waiting for the transporter list the save lands back on with the new transporter first and chosen.

claims.statement: Saving a commercial transporter's form lands on the transporter list, and saving that list reaches the overview.
claims.quote: - `fillAndSaveCommercialTransporterAddFormToOverview` fills and saves the open commercial transporter form, then saves the transporter list it lands on, reaching the overview — the one path specs that only need the overview, not the list's own state, take through the save.

claims.statement: The transporter list shows only the newest address-book entry of each name, so when two tests add a transporter of the same name at once the later add replaces the entry the earlier test's list chose, and that list's save is refused with "Select a transporter from the list".
claims.quote: Every test signs in to the same organisation, and its transporter list shows only the newest address-book entry of each name. When two tests add a transporter of the same name at once, the later add replaces the entry the earlier test's list chose, and that list's save is refused with "Select a transporter from the list".

claims.statement: The overview lists one set of task rows for a consignment that identifies an animal and travels by air or sea and another for an overland consignment, each in a fixed order the assertion exists to prove.
claims.quote: - `OVERLAND_OVERVIEW_TASKS` is the overview's task rows for an overland consignment, in the order the overview lists them. It is stated outright rather than derived from `AIR_OR_SEA_OVERVIEW_TASKS`, because the order is what the assertion that reads it exists to prove.

claims.statement: A rail consignment in transit passes the identification page with both of the chosen commodity's free-text fallback answers blank, because that commodity declares no identifier of its own and the two answers are optional.
claims.quote: - `walkPoultryByRail` walks a rail consignment in transit from creation to the review. It passes through the identification page straight after saving commodity details, leaving both of the chosen commodity's free-text fallback answers blank there, because the chosen commodity declares no identifier of its own and the two answers are optional.

claims.statement: The rail-poultry walk ends on the review rather than submitting, because the MDM stub serves no species page for that commodity and Continue from the review is refused.
claims.quote: It ends on the review rather than submitting, because the MDM stub serves no species page for this commodity and Continue from the review is refused.

claims.statement: A two-cat air consignment answers neither a county parish holding number nor the unweaned-animals question, because the commodity code cats share is not on the holding-number-required list and is not an unweaned code.
claims.quote: It answers neither a CPH number nor the unweaned-animals question, because the commodity code cats share is not on the CPH-required list (`CPH_REQUIRED_CODES`) and is not an unweaned code (`UNWEANED_CODES`).

claims.statement: The permanent address page is reached from the consignment addresses page, inside the leg of the journey that runs from the transporter to the review.
claims.quote: It answers the permanent address page from the consignment addresses page, which the walk reaches only inside `walkFromTransporterToReview`, so the caller's permanent-address step is supplied to that method rather than run before or after it.

claims.statement: The county parish holding number is answered on the consignment addresses page.
claims.quote: - `addCphAndLeaveAddresses` runs from the addresses page: it answers the CPH number and then leaves the page.

claims.statement: The animals API seed unlocks only origin and commodity, so a spec that needs the review walks the whole journey rather than seeding it.
claims.quote: - The API seed unlocks only origin and commodity, so a spec that needs the review walks the whole journey rather than seeding it. The walk's addresses leg picks the canned parties whose names and countries a review assertion reads.

claims.statement: A party picker refuses an address-book record that does not carry the role the picker is for, so each role's answer must name a record holding that role.
claims.quote: - `PartyNames` (`flows/animals/seed-form-steps.ts`) names the address-book record each role's answer picks. Every name must match a record `flows/shared/address-book-seed.ts` seeds holding that role, since a picker now refuses a record that does not carry its own role.

claims.statement: A party picker only threads its checked party through a server round trip, so a link off the page before that round trip carries the previously-saved party rather than the just-ticked one.
claims.quote: - `selectAndCommit` (`page-objects/animals/party-picker-page.ts`) ticks a party's radio, then re-searches to commit it: the picker only threads its checked party through a server round trip, so a link off the page before that round trip carries the previously-saved party, not the just-ticked one.

claims.statement: On the notification view a party's summary-list row is found by the card's title with the role as the row's term.
claims.quote: - `partyRow` selects the summary-list row of the card, found by its title, whose term is the role.

claims.statement: A summary card on the notification view offers a heading Change link and may offer a row link such as Edit details, and a card can hold a titled subsection such as "Permanent address" with its own summary list.
claims.quote: - `cardLinks` lists every link in a summary card, the heading Change link and any row link such as Edit details, so a spec can assert exactly which links a card offers. `editPartyDetails` finds the Edit details link on a party row. `cardSubsection` selects the summary list under a card's titled subsection, such as "Permanent address".

claims.statement: A summary list has no error state of its own, so an outstanding role carries its message in the row's value cell.
claims.quote: - `partyError` reads the first definition of the row. A summary list has no error state of its own, so an outstanding role carries its message in the row's value cell.

claims.statement: A species has no tick box on the commodity page until its own search lists it, and it is ticked inside the group for that species' own commodity code.
claims.quote: - `searchAndCheckSpecies` searches for each species before ticking it, because a species has no tick box until its own search lists it, and ticks it inside the group for the species' own commodity code.

claims.statement: The transit port of exit can be chosen by its code, so an assertion naming a particular port does not depend on the port list's order.
claims.quote: - `selectTransitPortOfExit` chooses the transit port of exit by its code, beside the by-position `selectTransitPortOfExitByIndex` that remains for a spec that only needs any port, so an assertion naming a particular port does not depend on the port list's order.
